L163@P5: often stands for a complete word. Even a seal with a single sign can
L164@P5: express its owner, and there is mostly little reason for sign repetition in
L165@P5: short seal texts written in an early logosyllabic script of the Sumerian type.
L166@P5: The alleged lack of what they call random-looking type of sign repetition
L167@P5: is mentioned as the fourth and most important and critical evidence
L168@P5: against the thesis that the Indus script is a writing system: ―Most
L169@P5: importantly, nowhere in Indus inscriptions do we find convincing
L170@P5: evidence of the random-looking types of sign repetition expected in
L171@P5: contemporary phonetic or semi-phonetic scripts‖ (Farmer & al. 2004: 29-
L172@P5: 30).
L173@P5: Farmer and his colleagues themselves admit that ―some Indus signs do
L174@P5: repeat in single inscriptions, sometimes including many repetions in a
L175@P5: row‖ (p. 31). However, they do not accept the evidence of such
L176@P5: duplications: ―Whatever the origins of these different types of
L177@P5: duplications, all that is critical for our purposes is to note again the lack of
L178@P5: any suggestions in them of the random-looking repetitions typical even of
L179@P5: monumental scripts like Luwian or Egyptian hieroglyphs‖ (p. 36).
L180@P5: The hieroglyphic signs drawn in black in fig. 1 mark the repetitions in the
L181@P5-6: cartouches of Ptolemy and Cleopatra; they were crucial in the Parpola, Asko 115
L182@P6: decipherment of the Egyptian script. But these are the repetitions when
L183@P6: both of the two cartouches are taken into consideration. Farmer and his
L184@P6: colleagues speak of sign repetitions limited to single cartouches, in which
L185@P6: case Ptolemy‘s cartouche has only one sign repetition, namely the
L186@P6: duplication of the sign E, one after the other in a row, which according to
L187@P6: Farmer & al. does not count as a "random-looking" repetition. Within
L188@P6: Cleopatra‘s cartouche, there is likewise only one sign repetition, namely
L189@P6: that of the eagle-shaped sign for A. This latter case would qualify as an
L190@P6: example of a ―random-looking‖ sign repetition.
L191@P6: Fig. 1 : Cartouches of Ptolemy and Cleopatra: the Egyptian hieroglyphs and their
L192@P6: transliterations (with repetitions shown in bold). (After Parpola 1994: 41, fig. 3.1.)
L193@P6: But sign repetition within single Indus inscription DOES occur, also of
L194@P6: the ―random-looking type" completely missed by Farmer and his
L195@P6: colleagues. Such repetition occurs even in the ―bar-seals‖, which Farmer
L196@P6: and his colleagues (2004: 33) consider particularly crucial for the Indus
L197@P6: script thesis. The following counter examples by no means exhaust the
L198@P6: material.
L199@P6: In the 10-sign text M-682 from Mohenjo-daro, one sign is repeated three
L200@P6: times, two other signs are repeated twice, and all in different places, that
L201@P6: is, not in a row.
L202@P6: In M-634 from Mohenjo-daro one sign is repeated in three different
L203@P6: places. Farmer and his colleagues have noticed this case, but disqualify it
L204@P6: because in their opinion the ―sun symbol‖ shows that non-linguistic
L205@P6: symbols are involved. Of course this sign can very well depict the solar
L206@P6: wheel with rays, as I have myself proposed on the basis of Near Eastern
L207@P6-7: and later Indian parallels (cf. Parpola 1994: 104, 106 fig. 7.5; 110; 116-116 Airāvati
L208@P7: 117). But, how do Farmer and his colleagues know that this sign has not
L209@P7: been used phonetically as a rebus sign: after all, it is precisely this type of
L210@P7: ―random repetition‖ that they consider as proof for phonetic usage!
L211@P7: In M-1792 (Marshall 1931: III, pl. 106 no. 93) from Mohenjo-daro one
L212@P7: sign (different from that of M-634) is also repeated in three different
L213@P7: places.
L214@P7: The seal K-10 from Kalibangan has ten signs. One and the same two-sign
L215@P7: sequence is repeated in two different places.
L216@P7: In the 11-sign text M-1169 from Mohenjo-daro, one sign is repeated in
L217@P7: two different places.
L218@P7: In the 8-sign "bar-seal" M-357 from Mohenjo-daro, one sign is repeated
L219@P7: in two different places.
L220@P7: I agree with Farmer and his colleagues that some of the sign duplications
L221@P7: in row imply quantification (cf. Farmer & al. 2004: 31). I shall come back
L222@P7: to the probable function of the small bifacial tablets later on. The
L223@P7: inscription on one side of them usually has just the U-shaped sign,
L224@P7: preceded by one to four vertical strokes for the numbers 1 to 4: UI, UII,
L225@P7: UIII, UIIII. In some tablets, such as H-764 from Harappa, the U-shaped
L226@P7: sign is repeated three times: UUU, obviously an alternative to UIII, where
L227@P7: III = number 3 is a numeral attribute (cf. Parpola 1994: 81). Farmer and
L228@P7: his colleagues want to deny the use of number signs as numeral attributes
L229@P7: of following signs; according to them they are independent symbols for
L230@P7: fixed conceptions: thus seven strokes should denote ―THE seven‖.
L231@P7: However, different numbers clearly alternate before certain signs, among
L232@P7: them the U-shaped sign, clearly suggesting attributive use (cf. Parpola
L233@P7: 1994: 81-82; 88; 120, fig. 7.21, I).
L234@P7: Farmer and his colleagues (2004: 31) surmise that the duplication of other
L235@P7: signs may emphasize their magical or political power. They do not
L236@P7: mention that such sign reduplications can reflect emphasizing linguistic
L237@P7: reduplications common in Dravidian (and other Indian languages)
L238@P7: especially in onomatopoeic words, or as grammatical markers, such as
L239@P7: Sumerian nominal plurals (cf. Parpola 1994: 82). There are also cases like
L240@P7: the reduplication of the sign ―dot-in-a-circle‘ that could depict the ‗eye‘.
L241@P7: Comparing the Dravidian words kaN ‗eye‘ and ka:N ‗to see‘, I have
L242@P7-8: proposed reading their reduplication as a compound word, namely kaNka:Ni attested in Tamil in the meaning ‗overseer‘, a meaning that would Parpola, Asko 117
L243@P8: suit very well for instance its occurrence on an ancient seal-impression on
L244@P8: a potsherd from Mohenjo-daro (M-1382) (cf. Parpola 1994: 215; 275).
L245@P8: "Lost" longer texts (manuscripts) never existed
L246@P8: All literary civilizations produced longer texts but there are none from the
L247@P8: Indus Valley — hence the Indus ―script‖ is no writing system: Farmer and
L248@P8: his colleagues reject the much repeated early assumption that longer texts
L249@P8: may have been written on ―birch bark, palm leaves, parchment, wood, or
L250@P8: cotton cloth, any of which would have perished in the course of ages‖ as
L251@P8: suggested by Sir John Marshall in 1931 (I, 39). Farmer and his colleagues
L252@P8: are ready to believe the ―Indus script thesis‖ only if an Indus text at least
L253@P8: 50 signs long is found.
L254@P8: But even though Farmer and his colleagues speak as if our present corpus
L255@P8: of texts was everything there ever existed, this is not the case. More than
L256@P8: 2100 Indus texts come from Mohenjo-daro alone, and yet less than one
L257@P8: tenth of that single city has been excavated. Farmer and his colleagues do
L258@P8: not know what has existed and what may be found in the remaining parts
L259@P8: of the city, even if it is likely that only imperishable material of the kinds
L260@P8: already available continue to be found. The Rongo-Rongo tablets of
L261@P8: Easter Island are much longer than 50 signs. But does this make it certain
L262@P8: that they represent writing in the strict sense?
L263@P8: Seed evidence shows that cotton has been cultivated in Greater Indus
L264@P8: Valley since Chalcolithic times, and cotton cloth is supposed to have been
L265@P8: one of the main export item of the Harappans. Yet all the millions of
L266@P8: Harappan pieces of cotton cloth have disappeared for climatic reasons,
L267@P8: save four cases where a few microscopic fibers have been preserved in
L268@P8: association with metal (cf. Possehl 2002: table 3.2, with further
L269@P8: references). Alexander‘s admiral Nearchus mentions ―thickly woven
L270@P8: cloth‖ used for writing letters in the Indus Valley c 325 BC. Sanskrit
L271@P8: sources such as the Ya:jñavalkya-Smrti (1,319) also mention cotton cloth,
L272@P8: (ka:rpa:sa-)paTa, as writing material around the beginning of the
L273@P8: Christian era. But the earliest preserved examples date from the 13th
L274@P8: century AD (cf. Shivaganesha Murthy 1996: 45-46; Salomon 1998: 132).
L275@P8: Emperor Asoka had long inscriptions carved on stone (pillars and rocks)
L276@P8: all around his wide realm in 260 to 250 BC. They have survived. But also
L277@P8: manuscripts on perishable materials must have existed in Asoka‘s times
L278@P8: and already since the Achaemenid rule started in the Indus Valley c 520
L279@P8: BC. This is suggested among other things by the mention of lipi ‗script‘
L280@P8-9: in Pa:Nini‘s Sanskrit Grammar (3,2,21) which is dated to around 400-350 118 Airāvati
L281@P9: BC. Sanskrit lipi comes from Old Persian dipi ‗script‘. The earliest
L282@P9: surviving manuscripts on birch bark, palm leaves and wooden blocks date
L283@P9: from the 2nd century AD and come from the dry climate of Central Asia
L284@P9: (cf. Shivaganesha Murthy 1996: 24-36; Salomon 1998: 131). We can
L285@P9: conclude that manuscripts on perishable materials have almost certainly
L286@P9: existed in South Asia during 600 years from the start of the Persian rule
L287@P9: onwards, but they have not been preserved; this period of 600 years with
L288@P9: no surviving manuscripts corresponds to the duration of the Indus
L289@P9: Civilization.
L290@P9: No cursive variant of the Indus script developed — hence no scribes
L291@P9: The sixth argument of Farmer and his colleagues is based on the
L292@P9: observation that everywhere scribes writing manuscripts tended to
L293@P9: develop a cursive style. From the fact that the Indus script changed very
L294@P9: little during its 600 years of existence they conclude that there were no
L295@P9: longer texts nor any scribes.
L296@P9: But the Egyptian hieroglyphs preserved their monumental pictographic
L297@P9: shapes for 3000 years.The Egyptian cursive hieratic style of papyrus
L298@P9: manuscripts does not differ so very much from the monumental
L299@P9: hieroglyphs. The difference between Maya manuscripts and monumental
L300@P9: inscriptions is not all that great, either.
L301@P9: Actually there is quite a lot of graphic variation in the Indus signs (see the
L302@P9: sign list in Parpola 1994: 70-78, fig. 5.1), and in my opinion this variation
L303@P9: provides also an important key to their pictorial or iconic understanding.
L304@P9: On the other hand, the Indus script emerges in the Mature Harappan
L305@P9: period already more or less fully standardized, and by this time a lot of
L306@P9: shape simplification or creation of a more cursive script had already taken
L307@P9: place.
L308@P9: No writing equipment has been found
L309@P9: No writing equipment has been found, hence Farmer and his colleagues
L310@P9: conclude that there were no scribes nor any manuscripts. Four
L311@P9: archaeologists specializing on the Indus Civilization have interpreted
L312@P9: some finds as writing equipment, but their suggestions ―are no longer
L313@P9: accepted by any active researchers‖ (Farmer et al. 2004: 25).
L314@P9: But thin metal rods, such as used in South India to incise palm leaf
L315@P9: manuscripts, could have early on corroded away or beyond recognition.
L316@P9-10: From painted Indus texts on Harappan pots (e.g. Sktd-3 from Surkotada Parpola, Asko 119
L317@P10: in CISI 1: p. 392) and bangles (cf. Blk-6 from Balakot in CISI 2: p. 432)
L318@P10: we know that Indus people used brushes to write, although such brushes
L319@P10: have not survived or have not been recognized — and in North India
L320@P10: palm leaf manuscripts have been painted with brushes. For the record,
L321@P10: some of the provisional identifications for Harappan writing equipment

L325@P10: The Indus "script" signs are actually non-linguistic symbols
L326@P10: Instead of a language-based writing system, Farmer and his colleagues
L327@P10: (2004: 45) see in the Indus signs ―a relatively simple system of religiouspolitical signs that could be interpreted in any language‖. The nonlinguistic symbols of Mesopotamian iconography are said to be a
L328@P10: particularly close and relevant parallel, as they may be arranged in regular
L329@P10: rows with a definite order like the Indus signs.
L330@P10: But in Mesopotamian seal iconography, the non-linguistic symbols
L331@P10: usually occur as isolated signs, for instance near the gods they belong to.
